title: Lines and words like a senior
summary: rg -w, counting blank lines, finding comments, showing the effective config with grep -v, editor search where ^ and $ are per line, and whole-word search in C#.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: lines and words
steps.body: Line tools search one line at a time, so `^` and `$` there always mean the start and end of a line. These are the anchor and boundary searches people run every week: on configs, on code before a rename, on files a formatter touched.

toolkit.what: Whole words only: rg wraps the pattern in word boundaries. Finds `id` but not `userId`, `ids` or `user_id`.
toolkit.when: before renaming a short identifier that also appears inside longer names

toolkit.what: Count blank lines in each file. Files with none are left out of the list.
flags: treat \r\n as the line end, so ^$ also finds blank lines in Windows files
toolkit.when: checking what a formatter or a bad merge did to a set of files

toolkit.what: Comment lines, with line numbers, even when indented. \s is a GNU extension; [[:space:]] is the portable POSIX class.
flags: start of line, optional whitespace, then #
POSIX spelling of \s: works in BSD and busybox grep too
toolkit.when: finding a setting someone commented out

toolkit.what: The effective config: drop blank lines and comment lines, keep what is actually set.
flags: invert: keep lines that do NOT match
toolkit.when: reviewing a server's real settings during an incident

toolkit.cmd: Ctrl+Shift+H (VS Code), regex on with Alt+R
toolkit.what: Find and replace across files. In regex mode ^ and $ match at every line; put \n in the pattern to match across lines.
flags: a blank line, including its newline
toolkit.example: Find: ^[ \t]*// TODO.*$   files to include: src/**/*.cs
toolkit.when: edits you want to preview and apply in one go

steps.prompt: Match each flag or piece of pattern to what it does.
pairs: keep the lines that do not match
treat `\r\n` as the end of a line
portable whitespace class for any grep

code: # show the settings sshd really uses: no comments, no blank lines
# how many blank lines does each Markdown file have?
steps.explain: The first needs both: `-v` to invert and `-E` so that `(#|$)` is a group with alternatives. Without `-E`, grep reads the brackets and the bar as plain characters. `-c` counts matching lines.

items: Find uses of the variable `id`, but not `userId` or `ids`

steps.title: Strip trailing whitespace
prompt: Code review asks you to remove trailing spaces and tabs from every line. Each match is replaced with nothing.
Write the pattern. Blank lines must stay: the file must keep exactly as many lines as it had.
hints: Spaces or tabs, one or more, right before the end of a line. The **m** flag makes `$` match at every line end.
Not `\s+$`: `\s` matches newlines too and swallows the blank line. Use `[ \t]+$`.
steps.explain: With `\s+$` the match runs from the end of `var x = 1;` through the blank line, and a line disappears from the diff. Windows files end lines with `\r\n`, and .NET's `$` only knows `\n`, so normalise line endings first.

steps.prompt: A teammate's C# code lists comment lines with `Regex.Matches(config, @"^#.*")`. It worked in VS Code search and with `grep '^#'`, but in C# it only ever returns the first comment. Why?
options: Without `RegexOptions.Multiline`, `^` matches only at the start of the whole text
`Regex.Matches` stops after the first match unless you call `NextMatch`
The file has Windows line endings
steps.explain: Line tools test one line at a time, so for them `^` is always the start of a line. `Regex.Matches` sees the whole file as one string, so you have to ask for per-line anchors with `RegexOptions.Multiline` (or `(?m)` at the front of the pattern).

The last one surprises people: one match for the blank line between `x` and `y`, and one at the very end, after the final newline, where `^` and `$` meet. `grep -c '^$'` would say 1. Counting blank lines with a .NET regex overcounts by one when the file ends with a newline.

steps.title: rg -w in C#
prompt: Write `int CountWord(string text, string word)`: how many times `word` appears in `text` as a whole word, ignoring
case, like `rg -wic`. The word comes from a user, so escape it.
Build the pattern as `@"\b" + Regex.Escape(word) + @"\b"` and count with `Regex.Count` and
(This works for words that start and end with a letter or digit. For `c++`, `\b` after the `+` needs a word character
next, which a space is not.) `System.Text.RegularExpressions` is already imported.
template: Dojo.Eq("id as a word: three times", 3, CountWord("id, userId, ids, _id, (id) user-id", "id"));
Dojo.Eq("ignores case, skips timeouts", 2, CountWord("Timeout, TIMEOUT and timeouts", "timeout"));
Dojo.Eq("the dot is literal and 1.20 is a different word", 1, CountWord("v1.2 v1.20 v1x2", "v1.2"));
Dojo.Eq("an empty text has none", 0, CountWord("", "id"));
hints: Put `\b` on both sides of the escaped word.
